title: Ram Kishore Gupta vs Mandip Singh on 22 December, 2023

Complainant case number 618029/2016 2. Name of the complainant Mr. Ram Kishore Gupta (Proprietor of Knits Fab India) R/o. 698/4B, Ground Floor, Gali No. 6, Adarsh Mohalla, Maujpur, Delhi-110053. Date of pronouncement 22.12.2023 -:JUDGEMENT:- 1. The present complaint under section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (herein referred to as NI Act ) has been filed by Mr. Ram Kishore Gupta (Proprietor of Knits Fab India) (herein referred to as the 'complainant') against Mr. Mandeep Singh (Proprietor of M/s Speed Apparels) (herein referred to as the 'accused'). Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.1 of19 2. Briefly stated, the case of the complainant is that complainant is carrying on supply of Hosiery Clothes under his proprietorship whereas the accused is the proprietor of M/s Speed Apparels and complainant and accused had business relations for long time and the complainant supplied to the accused on his order on credit basis as there was an understanding between both. That there are bills / invoices in respect of which part payment of which the cheque in question was issued are Ex.CW1/A-1 & 2. That in order to discharge his liability, the accused issued to the complainant, as consideration for previously supplied orders, a cheque bearing No. "010756" dated 05.11.2013 for Rs. 1,19,900/- drawn on Oriental Bank of Commerce, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065 which cheque is Ex.CW1/B. That in order to discharge his liability, accused paid Rs. 2,000/- to complainant on 18.12.2013 and further Rs. 10,000/- on 24.12.2013 seeking six months time to clear all dues pending and again accused issued to the complainant, as consideration for previously supplied orders, a post dated cheque bearing No. "000113" dated 24.06.2014 for Rs. 89,900/- drawn on Bank of India, East of Kailash Branch, D142, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065 which cheque is Ex.CW1/C. That when the said cheque was presented by the complainant for payment on the first time on 24.06.2014, it was returned unpaid with the remarks "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 27.06.2014. This fact was brought to notice of the accused by the complainant by way of telephone call, whereupon accused requested complainant to deposit the said cheque again and assured that the same shall be honoured by his banker. Copy of the return memo is Ex.CW1/D. That upon presentation for the second time on Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.2 of19 31.07.2014, the cheque was returned unpaid with the remarks "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 01.08.2014 which is Ex.CW1/E. This fact was brought to the notice of the accused by way of telephone call and accused again requested complainant to deposit the said cheque again with his banker and assured that it will be honoured upon presentation. Thereafter, complainant presented the cheque in question for third time on 11.09.2014 but to his dismay, the cheque was returned unpaid by the bank with the remarks "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 12.09.2014 which is Ex.CW1/F. That despite repeated telephone reminders and personal visit by the representative of the complainant to the accused, the accused failed to make the payment and did not bother about the request of the complainant and lingered on the matter on one pretext or the other. Thereafter, accused was duly served with the legal notice / demand notice dated 24.09.2014 sent through registered post which copy of legal notice / demand notice is Ex.CW1/G. Copy of the postal receipt for speed post is Ex.CW1/H and the tracking report is Ex.CW1/I. The accused failed to pay the amount mentioned on the cheque in question within the statutory period. Hence, the present complaint under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as ' NI Act ') was filed. 3. On issuance of summons, the counsel for accused entered appearance in the present matter for the first time on 02.01.2018 and the accused put in his personal appearance on 25.5.2018 and was admitted to bail. Notice u/s 251 CrPC was served upon the accused on 09.10.2018, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. His plea of defence was also recorded. Thereafter, the accused was allowed to cross-examine the complainant u/s Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.3 of19 145(2) NI Act . Thereafter, matter was listed for cross- examination of complainant for 07.12.2018 but on 07.12.2018, complainant failed to appear and last and final opportunity was granted to the complainant to pursue his complaint subject to cost of Rs. 1,000/- payable by complainant to accused on 20.02.2019. On 20.02.2019, complainant failed to appear and in the interest of justice, court issued court notice to the complainant as well as his counsel to pursue his complaint subject to cost of Rs. 3,000/- to be deposited by complainant with DLSA, South East, Saket for 22.04.2019. On 22.04.2019, complainant failed to appear and last and final opportunity was granted to the complainant to pursue his complaint and the court also issued court notice to complainant for taking steps for further prosecution of the case, failing which court would proceed on the basis of the evidence available on the record. On 03.07.2019 and 18.10.2019, complainant and accused were present, however their counsel were not present. On 28.01.2020, complainant failed to appear. On 05.03.2021 complainant remained absent and it was observed that complainant is not appearing before the court regularly and in the interest of justice, one more opportunity was provided to the complainant to appear before the court failing which, complaint case would be dismissed for non-prosecution. The court even issued notice to the complainant. On 17.12.2021, again complainant was absent. On 02.03.2022, matter was at the stage of CE but complainant appeared through VC and matter was adjourned. Thereafter, on 26.07.2022 complainant and accused were present but their respective counsels were not present. On 15.10.2022, complainant and accused were present with counsel for complainant, however, no effective steps were Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.4 of19 taken to conduct CE. On 06.12.2022, complainant was present with counsel but accused was absent. On 06.04.2023 one appeared. On 06.06.2023 complainant was absent and adjournment was sought by his counsel for CE due to unavailability of complainant. On 23.08.2023, complainant was absent whereas accused was present and the matter was listed for CE for 07.10.2023. On 07.10.2023, this court observed that complainant had neither paid the cost as imposed on 07.12.2018 nor deposited the cost imposed on 20.02.2019 and directed the complainant who was present in the court to pay the cost but even on that day, complainant was not ready to pay the cost despite there being a direction dated 20.02.2019 upon the complainant that the CE shall be subject to cost. In view of this, CE was closed on 07.10.2023 as complainant was not complying with the court orders since last five years and was remaining absent on one date or the other while lingering on the matter. Thereafter, matter was fixed for recording statement of accused and the same was recorded on 01.11.2023, whereas even on 01.11.2023 complainant was absent. Thereafter, since accused did not choose to lead DE, matter was fixed for final arguments for 15.12.2023. On 15.12.2023, complainant remained absent and final arguments were heard on behalf of the accused, while considering the conduct of the complainant writ large, the right of the complainant to address final arguments was closed and matter was reserved for judgment. APPLICABLE LAW:- 5. Before appreciating the facts of the case in detail for the purpose of decision, let relevant position of law be discussed. Now, Section 138 Negotiable Instrument Act provides as under: Section 138 . Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months (reduced to three months vide notification no. RBI/201112/251, DBOD AMLBCNo. 47/19.01.0062011/12,dated Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.8 of19 04.11.2011) from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation -- for the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under S.138 N.I. Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: (1) drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, for payment to another person from out of that account for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; (2) cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months (now three months) from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; (3) returning the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque, (4) giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount, (5) failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. Being cumulative, it is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 of the N I Act. The Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque i.e. Complainant in the present case; firstly, in regard to the passing of consideration as contained in Section 118 (a) therein and, secondly, a presumption under Section 139 , that the holder of cheque receiving the same of the nature referred to in Section 138 for discharge, Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.9 of19 in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa , AIR 2019 SC 1983, noted at para 23 as follows [ Bharat Barrel and Drum Manufacturing Company v. Amin Chand Pyarelal , (1999) 3 SCC 35; M.S. Narayana Menon alias Mani v. State of Kerala and another , (2006) 6 SCC 39; Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde, (2008) 4 SCC 54; Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513; Rangappa v. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 referred]: (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. (iii) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. (iv) That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. (v) It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence. To put in nutshell, the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 N.I. Act,is that the presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The onus to prove the issuance of the cheque lies upon the complainant, and the same has to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, unless the accused admits the same. Once the issuance of cheque is established, either by Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.10 of19 admission or by positive evidence, the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 arises. We can summarize the general principles in the following way: Onus of proof: Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 states that it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 , for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Therefore, here the onus shifts upon the accused to prove the nonexistence of debt or other liability. Section 139 of the N.I. Act uses the word "shall presume", which means that the presumption under Section 139 is rebuttable. Standard of proof: The standard of proof required to rebut the presumption under Section 139 is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or other liability, the onus shifts back to the complainant to prove by way of evidence, beyond reasonable doubt, that the cheque in question was issued by the accused in discharge, whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, and now the presumptions under Section 118 (a) and Section 139 will not come to the aid of the complainant. Mode of Proof: The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the cheque in question was not supported by consideration, and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the Court need not insist in every case that the accused should prove the nonexistence of the consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that a bare denial of passing of consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances upon the consideration of which, the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist, or their nonexistence was so probable that a prudent man would, under circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.11 of19 As discussed above, from the legal provisions and the law laid down in various judgments, it can be safely gathered that it is for the accused to rebut the presumptions. He can do so by cross examining the complainant, leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. It is amply clear that the accused does not need to discharge his or her liability beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. He just needs to create holes in the case set out by the complainant. Accused can say that the version brought forth by the complainant is inherently unbelievable and therefore the prosecution cannot stand. In this situation the accused has nothing to do except to point inherent inconsistency in the version of the complainant or the accused can give his version of the story and say that on the basis of his version the story of the complainant cannot be believed. ARGUMENTS AND APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE:- 6. No arguments were led on behalf of the complainant. Accordingly, complaint is being disposed off in terms of its own merits. Whereas, final arguments were advanced on behalf of the accused. 7. It is submitted as per the complaint that the accused has issued the cheque bearing his signature on the cheque in the present case, thus, the presumptions u/s 118 (a) read with Section 139 of NI Act about the cheque in question having been issued for consideration and in discharge of legal liability should arise in favor of the complainant. That the complainant was carrying on supply of Hosiery Clothes under his proprietorship whereas the accused was the proprietor of M/s Speed Apparels and complainant and accused had business relations for long time and the complainant supplied to the accused on his order on credit basis as there was an understanding between both. That there are bills / invoices in respect of which part payment of which the Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.12 of19 cheque in question was issued are Ex.CW1/A-1 & 2. That in order to discharge his liability, the accused issued to the complainant, as consideration for previously supplied orders, a cheque bearing No. "010756" dated 05.11.2013 for Rs. 1,19,900/- drawn on Oriental Bank of Commerce, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065 which cheque is Ex.CW1/B. That in order to discharge his liability, accused paid Rs. 2,000/- to complainant on 18.12.2013 and further Rs. 10,000/- on 24.12.2013 seeking six months time to clear all dues pending and again accused issued to the complainant, as consideration for previously supplied orders, a post dated cheque bearing No. "000113" dated 24.06.2014 for Rs. 89,900/- drawn on Bank of India, East of Kailash Branch, D142, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065 which cheque is Ex.CW1/C. That when the said cheque was presented by the complainant for payment on the first time on 24.06.2014, it was returned unpaid with the remarks "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 27.06.2014. That this fact was brought to notice of the accused by the complainant by way of telephone call, whereupon accused requested complainant to deposit the said cheque again and assured that the same shall be honoured by his banker. Copy of the return memo is Ex.CW1/D. That upon presentation for the second time on 31.07.2014, the cheque was returned unpaid with the remarks "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 01.08.2014 which is Ex.CW1/E. This fact was brought to the notice of the accused by way of telephone call and accused again requested complainant to deposit the said cheque again with his banker and assured that it will be honoured upon presentation. Thereafter, complainant presented the cheque in question for third time on 11.09.2014 but Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.13 of19 to his dismay, the cheque was returned unpaid by the bank with the remarks "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 12.09.2014 which is Ex.CW1/F. That despite repeated telephone reminders and personal visit by the representative of the complainant to the accused, the accused failed to make the payment and did not bother about the request of the complainant and lingered on the matter on one pretext or the other. Thereafter, accused was duly served with the legal notice / demand notice dated 24.09.2014 sent through registered post which copy of legal notice / demand notice is Ex.CW1/G. Copy of the postal receipt for speed post is Ex.CW1/H and the tracking report is Ex.CW1/I. That the accused failed to pay the amount mentioned on the cheque in question within the statutory period, hence, the accused is liable to be convicted under Section 138 NI Act. Per contra, it is submitted on behalf of the accused that the cheque in question although bears the signature of the accused, however, the same was merely a security cheque as the complainant approached the accused showing a brochure of certain hosiery fabrics and represented to the accused that the complainant can develop the same. The accused agreed for the development of the fabric and also handed over the security cheque demanded by the complainant for developing the fabric but the accused did not supply any goods to the complainant qua the cheque in question. That the complainant concocted a story to suit his theme. Complainant failed to put himself under cross- examination and did not enter the witness box to give even an opportunity to the accused to test his credibility. That the complainant had misused the cheque in question after obtaining the same from the accused by pressurizing him but supplied no Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.14 of19 goods and therefore there was no liability qua the cheque in question upon the accused. That the presumption under Section 139 of NI Act, should not arise. The three-Judge Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 has held that: "where the fact of signature on the cheque is acknowledged, a presumption has to be raised that the cheque pertained to a legally enforceable debt or liability, however, this presumption is of a rebuttal nature and the onus is then on the accused to raise a probable defence." 8. In the present case, the accused has not denied his signature on the cheque Ex.CW1/C. The factum of signature of the accused on the cheque by the accused is not disputed and has been acknowledged. 9. It is pertinent to mention here that Section 139 only raises the presumption on fulfillment of its conditions that the cheque was issued for discharge of in whole or in part any debt or other liability but there is no presumption as to the existence of the debt or liabilty as such. In Rangappa (supra) it has been held that : "Existence of legally recoverable debt is not a matter of presumption under Section 139 of the Act. It merely raises a presumption in favour of a holder of the cheque that the same has been issued for discharge of any debt or other liability." 10. As regards the legal notice, the receipt of the same has been denied by the accused at the time of framing of notice on 09.10.2018. It is pertinent to note that the accused stated during statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. that the address i.e. 212-A, Basement, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110056 mentioned on the legal notice i.e. Ex.CW1/G is incorrect and that Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.15 of19 his actual address is 112-A, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065. As per Postal receipt i.e. Ex.CW1/H and tracking report Ex.CW1/I, legal demand notice Ex.CW1/G was duly sent to the accused, however, it is pertinent to note that the bills / invoices relied upon by the complainant mentions the address 112-A, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065, hence the complainant has mentioned not only the wrong house number on the demand notice Ex.CW1/G but also the wrong PIN Code number on the demand notice Ex.CW1/G. Although, Ex.CW1/H mentions the PIN Code 110065, however, the house number is not mentioned on the postal receipt, hence it is not clear whether the complainant sent the demand notice to the incorrect address mentioned on the legal notice. As per provisions of Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872, read with Section 27 of General Clauses Act, the court may presume that legal notice duly addressed to the accused person and dispatched to him by way of post was actually received by the accused person, regard being had to common course of natural events. Reliance is also placed upon the case of C C Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed [2007 (6) SCC 555] wherein it was held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that: "it is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of criminal law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons and therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court alongwith the copy of Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.16 of19 the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of General Clauses Act and Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act." Considering the fact that the complainant has mentioned the wrong address on the legal demand notice Ex.CW1/G which is inconsistent with his own bills / invoices Ex.CW1/A-1 and Ex.CW1/A-2, this court is not inclined to presume the service of the legal demand notice Ex.CW1/G upon the accused as wrong house number and wrong PIN Code have been mentioned upon the legal demand notice. 11. As regards to the fact of dishonor of the cheque in question, the original return memos Ex.CW1/D, Ex.CW1/E and Ex.CW1/F filed by the complainant clearly show that the cheque in question Ex.CW-1/C was dishonored for the reasons 'Funds Insufficient'. In the case at hand, neither any argument has been raised on behalf of the accused to dispute the dishonor of the cheque nor this fact has been denied at any stage of the matter. Thus, taking into account that dishonor of cheque is not disputed, this fact, stands proved. 12. Thus, the presentation of the cheque in question and its dishonor is proved, however, the complainant has failed to prove the service of legal notice upon the accused. Consequently, the complainant has failed to raise a presumption under Section 139 NI Act since the service of legal demand notice in terms of Section 138 Proviso (b) NI Act has not been proved by the complainant. Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.17 of19 Accordingly, it cannot be presumed that the cheque in question was drawn for consideration and the holder of the cheque i.e., the complainant received the same in discharge of an existing debt as the essential ingredient as provided by Proviso (b) of Section 138 NI Act has not been fulfilled, hence the offence under Section 138 NI Act cannot be attracted against the accused. The accused at the time of recording of his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. brought the attention of the court to the discrepancy in the address mentioned on the legal notice i.e. Ex.CW1/G wherein, house number and PIN Code of the accused 112-A, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110065 are wrongly mentioned as 212-A, Basement, Sant Nagar, East of Kailash, New Delhi-110056. Therefore, accused has successfully been able to demolish even the drawing of presumption against him as per Sections 118 / 139 NI Act as the complainant failed to prove the service of legal demand notice upon the accused. 13. It is a settled position that the accused has to rebut the presumption raised under Section 139 and the standard of proof of which is 'preponderance of probabilities'. It is for the accused to raise a probable defence which creates a doubt on the version of the complainant. In the present case, presumption under Section 139 NI Act has not been attracted as not only complainant failed to enter the witness box for the purpose of cross-examination by the accused but also failed to prove the service of legal demand notice upon the accused which is an essential ingredient under Section 138 NI Act so as to attract the offence against the accused. The accused, in the present matter has succeeded in creating a doubt on the version of the Ct. Case No. 618029/2016 Ram Kishore Gupta vs. Mandeep Singh Page No.18 of19 complainant. The accused has demolished the allegation of service of legal notice by showing material contradiction in the address mentioned on the legal demand notice and the address mentioned on the bills / invoices relied upon by the complainant and has seriously brought into question the bonafide of the complainant. DECISION:- 14. Resultantly, the accused is acquitted of the alleged offence under section 138 of NI act. Announced in the open court today on 22nd December, 2023.
